prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, bringing atomic time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a single, identifiable idea (state-insensitive trapping of many atoms at a magic wavelength) that was turned into the most accurate measurement instrument yet built. Katori supplied the concept and first realisation, and Ye's group took it to the 10^-18 regime and used it to probe many-body effects, gravitational redshift at millimetre scales and constants variation. Independent laboratories now reproduce the performance and compare clocks across continents, so the result does not rest on one group. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: two names, theory-and-first-demonstration plus record-accuracy realisation, with no obvious third claimant forced out by the three-person limit. Three members placed it first and six placed it in their top three, and I think that reflects the discovery rather than a convenient configuration, since unlike several rivals it does not need the committee to resolve a contested credit line.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the formal redefinition of the second has not happened, so a prize could be read as anticipating a decision that belongs to metrology bodies, and that the lattice clock builds on ground already honoured in 2005 (frequency combs) and 2012 (single-ion control and optical clocks). Other groups at PTB, NIST, SYRTE and elsewhere pushed lattice clocks forward in parallel, so the line around Katori and Ye is not as sharp as the two-name credit suggests. Finally, the risk of being biased by my own field is real: I know how much hinges on atomic-structure inputs such as polarisabilities and blackbody shifts, and I may overweight them.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first because the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 Jarillo-Herrero discovery is a convincing theory-experiment pair, robustly reproduced and timely after about eight years, while he places the optical lattice clock only fifth as outside his area.
responses.response: I agree that the theory-plus-experiment structure of B013 is persuasive and I ranked it third myself. My qualification is about credit, not merit: Bistritzer and MacDonald are not interchangeable with Jarillo-Herrero's group, and Andrei's earlier STM evidence for flat-band physics is exactly what makes the three-person cut hard; the committee would have to say publicly who it left out. I also do not accept that a still-open superconducting pairing mechanism is irrelevant to timing, since the prize would rest on a field in rapid motion. The clock result has no comparable open question about what was discovered, only a pending administrative redefinition, which does not affect the physics. I would not call B013 unworthy, just less settled in attribution than B001.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks topological insulators (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) first as a mature, overdue field with extensive confirmation, and places optical lattice clocks fifth because the redefinition of the second is pending and other groups and earlier ion-clock work contributed.
responses.response: I take the maturity and impact of topological insulators seriously and ranked B024 fourth. But I disagree that a pending redefinition lowers the clock case: the discovery is the demonstration of 10^-18 accuracy and reproducibility, which is already settled, whereas the redefinition is a policy step that follows. I also think B024 has the harder attribution problem. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe effect and are outside the credited names, and Hasan's three-dimensional observations are credited yet would be excluded from Pearce's own trio. I am open to hearing whether Pearce sees the HgTe prediction as separable from Kane-Mele and Molenkamp; if so, B024 moves up for me, but I do not see that yet.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the architecture underlying essentially all superconducting quantum processors, mature and independently confirmed, while acknowledging his own bias as someone working in the area.
responses.response: I agree cQED is a real invention and I drew the analogy to cavity QED when ranking it fifth. My reservation is timing and allocation: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits went to Clarke, Devoret and Martinis, and Devoret, Nakamura and Girvin are all adjacent to the architecture, with the transmon work of Koch, Schreier and others also outside the credited trio. Awarding cQED so soon after would make the overlap hard to explain. I would not discard it for a later year, but I do not think it should displace the clock this round.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks twisted bilayer graphene first as a transparent, controllable platform for strongly correlated many-body physics, and places the optical lattice clock second as a clear invention with mature, multi-laboratory confirmation.
responses.response: I am glad that Mehlig's view of the clock matches mine: strong confirmation, good timing and a natural two-person credit. Where I differ is on how much the controllable-platform argument carries for B013, because a platform whose central physical question, the origin of the superconductivity, is unresolved is a weaker case than a measurement whose accuracy is directly demonstrated. I would be willing to support B013 as a second choice if the committee wants a condensed-matter prize in this year's discussion.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer to wait for the redefinition of the second before honouring optical clocks.
How sharply Katori's priority on the magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's accuracy leadership separate from the work of other lattice-clock groups; I am relying on memory for the exact chronology.
Whether a second, distinct achievement could be sensibly combined with the clock under the three-person limit, since only one or at most one additional person would remain.
Whether the HgTe prediction can be separated from Kane-Mele and Molenkamp, which bears on how strongly B024 should be considered as an alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. My documented collaborations (L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Keller's group at ETH, Schuch, Dahlström, Argenti, Indelicato) concern attosecond and highly charged ion physics, not optical lattice clocks, and none of those collaborators is a credited name on this shortlist. My field of atomic theory is close to clock physics, which I disclose as a possible bias but not a recusal issue.
